BIBLIOGRAPHIC RECORD

James Wood, comp.  Dictionary of Quotations.  1899.

Carlyle

A fact is a great thing: a sentence printed, if not by God, then at least by the Devil.
“A fair day’s wages for a fair day’s work,” is as just a demand as governed men ever made of governing; yet in what corner of this planet was that ever realised?
A lie should be trampled on and extinguished wherever found.
A man cannot be in the seventeenth century and the nineteenth at one and the same moment.His experience while editing Cromwell’s Letters.
A man is not born the second time, any more than the first, without travail.
A man is not strong who takes convulsion fits, though six men cannot hold him; only he that can walk under the heaviest weight without staggering.
A man lives by believing something; not by debating and arguing about many things.
A man must verify or expel his doubts, and convert them into certainty of Yes 
or
 No.
A man protesting against error is on the way towards uniting himself with all men that believe in truth.
A man who cannot gird himself into harness will take no weight along these highways.
A man who does not know rigour cannot pity either.
A man with half a volition goes backwards and forwards, and makes no way on the smoothest road.
A man, be the heavens praised, is sufficient for himself; yet were ten men, united in love, capable of being and doing what ten thousand singly would fail in.
A thinking man is the worst enemy the Prince of Darkness can have.
A well-written life is almost as rare as a well-spent one.
A word spoken in season, at the right moment, is the mother of ages.
A world all sincere, a believing world; the like has been; the like will again be—cannot help being.
All balloons give up their gas in the pressure of things, and collapse in a sufficiently wretched manner erelong.
All deep joy has something of awful in it.
All destruction, by violent revolution or howsoever it be, is but new creation on a wider scale.
All evil is as a nightmare; the instant you begin to 
stir
 under it, the evil is gone.
All great peoples are conservative.
All history is an inarticulate Bible.
All inmost things are melodious, naturally utter themselves in song.
All living objects do by necessity form to themselves a skin.
All men, if they work not as in the great taskmaster’s eye, will work wrong.
All objects are as windows through which the philosophic eye looks into infinitude.
All speech, even the commonest, has something of song in it.
All talent, all intellect, is in the first place moral.
All that mankind has done, thought, gained, or been, it is all lying in magic preservation in the pages of books.
All true men are soldiers in the same army, to do battle against the same enemy—the empire of darkness and wrong.
All, were it only a withered leaf, works together with all.
Always there is a black spot in our sunshine, the shadow of ourselves.
“Am I to be saved? or am I to be lost?” Certain to be lost, so long as you put that question.
An irreverent knowledge is no knowledge; it may be a development of the logical or other handicraft faculty, but is no culture of the soul of a man.
As a priest, or interpreter of the holy, is the noblest and highest of all men; so is a sham priest the falsest and basest.
Authors are martyrs, witnesses to the truth, or else nothing.
Bad is by its very nature negative, and can do nothing; whatsoever enables us to do anything, is by its very nature good.
Be thankful for your ennui; it is your last mark of manhood.
Beautiful it is to understand and know that a thought did never yet die; that as thou, the originator thereof, hast gathered it and created it from the whole past, so thou wilt transmit to the whole future.
Bees will not work except in darkness; thought will not work except in silence; neither will virtue work except in secrecy.
Big destinies of nations or of persons are not founded 
gratis
 in this world.
Biography is the most universally pleasant, the most universally profitable, of all reading.
Biography is the only true history.
Blessed is he that continueth where he is; here let us rest and lay out seed-fields; here let us learn to dwell.
Blessed is the voice that, amid dispiritment, stupidity, and contradiction, proclaims to us, Euge! (
i.e.,
 Excellent! Bravo!).
Books still accomplish miracles; they persuade men.
By any ballot-box, Jesus Christ goes just as far as Judas Iscariot.
By nature man hates change; seldom will he quit his old home till it has actually fallen about his ears.
By pious heroic climbing of our own, not by arguing with our poor neighbours, wandering to right and left, do we at length reach the sanctuary—the victorious summit, and see with our own eyes.
“Can” and “shall,” well understood, mean the same thing under this sun of ours.
Can I choose my king? I can choose my King Popinjay, and play what farce or tragedy I may with him; but he who is to be my ruler, whose will is higher than my will, was chosen for me in heaven.
Cant is properly a double-distilled lie, the second power of a lie.
Cast forth thy act, thy word, into the ever-living, ever-working universe. It is a seed-grain that cannot die; unnoticed to-day, it will be found flourishing as a banyan-grove, perhaps, alas! as a hemlock forest, after a thousand years.
Celebrity is but the candle-light which will show 
what
 man, not in the least make him a better or other man.
Clothes have made men of us; they are threatening to make clothes-screens of us.
Complaining profits little; stating of the truth may profit.
Condemnable idolatry is insincere idolatry—a human soul clinging spasmodically to an Ark of the Covenant, which it half feels is now a phantasm.
Contempt is a dangerous element to sport in; a deadly one, if we habitually live in it.
Conversion is the awakening of a soul to see into the awful 
truth
 of things; to see that Time and its shows all rest on Eternity, and this poor earth of ours is the threshold either of heaven or hell.
Conversion—a grand epoch for a man; properly the one epoch; the turning-point which guides upwards, or guides downwards, him and his activities for evermore.
Conviction, never so excellent, is worthless till it convert itself into conduct.
Creation is great, and cannot be understood.
Culture (is the process by which a man) becomes all that he was created capable of being, resisting all impediments, casting off all foreign, especially all noxious, adhesions, and showing himself at length in his own shape and stature, be these what they may.
Curious to think how, for every man, any the truest fact is modelled by the nature of the man.
Custom doth make dotards of us all.
Death is but another phasis of life, which also is awful, fearful, and wonderful, reaching to heaven and hell.
Democracy is, by the nature of it, a self-cancelling business, and gives in the long-run a net result of zero.
Despotism is essential in most enterprises; I am told they do not tolerate “freedom of debate” on board a seventy-four.
Difficult to sweep the intricate foul chimneys of law.
Difficulty, abnegation, martyrdom, death, are the allurements that act on the heart of man. Kindle the inner genial life of him, you have a flame that burns up all lower considerations.
Dilettantism, hypothesis, speculation, a kind of amateur-search for truth, toying and coquetting with truth; this is the sorest sin, the root of all imaginable sins.
Diligent, that includes all virtues in it a student can have.
To the Students of Edinburgh University.
Disorder is dissolution, death.
Divine 
right,
 take it on the great scale, is found to mean divine 
might
 withal.
Divine moment, when over the tempest-tossed soul, as over the wild-weltering chaos, it was spoken: Let there be Light. Even to the greatest that has felt such a moment, is it not miraculous and God-announcing; even as, under simpler figures, to the humblest and least?
Do the duty which lies nearest to thee. Thy second duty will already have become clearer.
Do we not all submit to death? The highest sentence of the law, sentence of death, is passed on all of us by the fact of birth; yet we live patiently under it, patiently undergo it when the hour comes.
Does Homer interest us now, because he wrote of what passed beyond his native Greece, and two centuries before he was born; or because he wrote what passed in God’s world, which is the same after thirty centuries?
Don’t hate; only pity and avoid those that follow lies.
Double, double toil and trouble; that is the life of all governors that really govern; not the spoil of victory, only the glorious toil of battle can be theirs.
Dupes indeed are many; but of all dupes there is none so fatally situated as he who lives in undue terror of being duped.
Each human heart can properly exhibit but one love, if even one; the “first love, which is infinite,” can be followed by no second like unto it.
Each one of us here, let the world go how it will, and be victorious or not victorious, has he not a life of his own to lead?
Efforts, to be permanently useful, must be uniformly joyous,—a spirit all sunshine,—graceful from very gladness,—beautiful because bright.
Egoism is the source and summary of all faults and miseries whatsoever.
Endeavouring, by logical argument, to prove the existence of God, were like taking out a candle to look for the sun.
After Kant.
Enjoying things which are pleasant, that is not the evil; it is the reducing of our moral self to slavery by them that is.
Ere we censure a man for seeming what he is not, we should be sure that we know what he is.
Eternity looks grander and kinder if Time grow meaner and more hostile.
Ever must pain urge us to labour, and only in free effort can any blessedness be imagined for us.
Ever must the sovereign of mankind be fitly entitled king, 
i.e.,
 the man who 
kens
 and 
can.
Ever, as of old, the thing a man will do is the thing he feels commanded to do.
Every conceivable society may well be figured as properly and wholly a Church, in one or other of these three predicaments: an audibly preaching and prophesying Church, which is the best; a Church that struggles to preach and prophesy, but cannot as yet till its Pentecost come; a Church gone dumb with old age, or which only mumbles delirium prior to dissolution.
Every man carries within him a potential madman.
Every man, within that inconsiderable figure of his, contains a whole spirit-kingdom and reflex of the All; and, though to the eye but some six standard feet in size, reaches downwards and upwards, unsurveyable, fading into the regions of immensity and eternity.
Every mortal longs for his parade-place; would still wish, at banquets, to be master of some seat or other wherein to overtop this or that plucked goose of the neighbourhood.
Every new opinion, at its starting, is precisely in a minority of one.
Every noble crown is, and on earth will ever be, a crown of thorns.
Every noble work is at first impossible.
Every poet, be his outward lot what it may, finds himself born in the midst of prose; he has to struggle from the littleness and obstruction of an actual world into the freedom and infinitude of an ideal.
Everywhere in life the true question is, not what we gain, but what we do; so also in intellectual matters it is not what we receive, but what we are made to give, that chiefly contents and profits us.
Everywhere the formed world is the only habitable one.
Everywhere the human soul stands between a hemisphere of light and another of darkness; on the confines of two everlasting, hostile empires, Necessity and Free Will.
Evil and good are everywhere, like shadow and substance; (for men) inseparable, yet not hostile, only opposed.
Evil, what we call evil, must ever exist while man exists; evil, in the widest sense we can give it, is precisely the dark, disordered material out of which man’s freewill has to create an edifice of order and good. Ever must pain urge us to labour; and only in free effort can any blessedness be imagined for us.
Except by mastership and servantship, there is no conceivable deliverance from tyranny and slavery.
Except in obedience to the heaven-chosen is freedom not so much as conceivable.
Experience is the grand spiritual doctor.
Experience takes dreadfully high school-wages, but teaches as no other.
Eyes bright, with many tears behind them.
On his Wife.
Facts—historical facts, still more biographical—are sacred hierograms, for which the fewest have the key.
Faith has given man an inward willingness, a world of strength wherewith to front a world of difficulty.
Faith is loyalty to some inspired teacher, some spiritual hero.
Falsehood is our one enemy in this world.
Falsehood is the essence of all sin.
Fame, we may understand, is no sure test of merit, but only a probability of such: it is an accident, not a property, of a man; like light, it can give little or nothing, but at most may show what is given; often it is but a false glare, dazzling the eyes of the vulgar, lending, by casual extrinsic splendour, the brightness and manifold glance of the diamond to pebbles of no value.
Fantasy is the true heaven-gate and hell-gate of man.
Fiction, while the feigner of it knows that he is feigning, partakes, more than we suspect, of the nature of lying; and has ever an, in some degree, unsatisfactory character.
Fidelity, diligence, decency, are good and indispensable; yet, without faculty, without light, they will not do the work.
Fight on, thou brave true heart, and falter not, through dark fortune and through bright, the cause thou lightest for, so far as it is true, is very sure of victory.
Find mankind where thou wilt, thou findest it in living movement, in progress faster or slower; the phœnix soars aloft, hovers with outstretched wings, filling earth with her music; or, as now, she sinks, and with spheral swan-song immolates herself in flame, that she may soar the higher and sing the clearer.
Finding your able man, and getting him invested with the symbols of ability, is the business, well or ill accomplished, of all social procedure whatsoever in this world.
Fire is the best of servants; but what a master!
First must the dead letter of religion own itself dead, and drop piecemeal into dust, if the living spirit of religion, freed from its charnel-house, is to arise in us, new-born of heaven, and with new healing under its wings.
Follow the devil faithfully, you are sure to go to the devil.
For a genuine man it is no evil to be poor.
For all right judgment of any man or thing it is useful, nay, essential, to see his good qualities before pronouncing on his bad.
For ever is not a category that can establish itself in this world of time.
For man’s well-being faith is properly the one thing needful; with it, martyrs, otherwise weak, can cheerfully endure the shame and the cross; and without it, worldlings puke up their sick existence by suicide in the midst of luxury.
For one man who can stand prosperity, there are a hundred that will stand adversity.
For suffering and enduring there is no remedy but striving and doing.
For the son of man there is no noble crown, well-worn or even ill-worn, but is a crown of thorns.
For thee the family of man has no use; it rejects thee; thou art wholly as a dissevered limb: so be it; perhaps it is better so.
Carlyle, or Teufelsdröckh rather, arrived at the “Centre of Indifference, through which whoso travels from the Negative Pole to the Positive must necessarily pass.”
Forms which grow round a substance will be true, good; forms which are consciously put round a substance, bad.
Formulas are the very skin and muscular tissue of a man’s life; and a most blessed indispensable thing, so long as they have vitality withal, and are a living skin and tissue to him.
Friend, hast thou considered the “rugged, all-nourishing earth,” as Sophocles well names her; now she feeds the sparrow on the housetop, much more her darling, man?
Friendship, in the old heroic sense of that term, no longer exists; except in the cases of kindred or other legal affinity, it is in reality no longer expected or recognised as a virtue among men.
From every moral death there is a new birth; / in this wondrous course of his, man may indeed linger, but cannot retrograde or stand still.
From the lowest depth there is a path to the loftiest height.
General suffering is the fruit of general misbehaviour, general dishonesty.
Generations are as the days of toilsome mankind; death and birth are the vesper and the matin bells that summon mankind to sleep, and to rise refreshed for new advancement.
Genius has privileges of its own; it selects an orbit for itself; and be this never so eccentric, if it is indeed a celestial orbit, we mere star-gazers must at last compose ourselves, must cease to cavil at it, and begin to observe it and calculate its laws.
Genius is ever a secret to itself.
Genius is the transcendent capacity of taking trouble first of all.
Genius will reconcile men to much.
Ghosts! There are nigh a thousand million walking the earth openly at noontide; some half-hundred have vanished from it, some half-hundred have arisen in it, ere thy watch ticks once.
Gift of prophecy has been wisely denied to man. Did a man foresee his life, and not merely hope it and grope it, and so by necessity and free-will make and fabricate it into a reality, he were no man, but some other kind of creature, superhuman or subterhuman.
Give us the man who sings at his work! Be his occupation what it may, he will be equal to any of those who follow the same pursuit in silent sullenness. He will do more in the same time; he will do it better; he will persevere longer.
Given a living man, there will be found clothes for him; he will find himself clothes; but the suit of clothes pretending that it is both clothes and man.
Given a world of knaves, to educe an Honesty from their united action, is a problem that is becoming to all men a palpably hopeless one.
Given the men a people choose, the people itself, in its exact worth and worthlessness, is given.
Go deep enough, there is music everywhere.
God is, nay, alone is; for with like emphasis we cannot say that anything else is.
“Godlike men love lightning;” godless men love it not; shriek murder when they see it, shutting their eyes, and hastily putting on smoked spectacles.
Goethe’s devil is a cultivated personage and acquainted with the modern sciences; sneers at witchcraft and the black art even while employing them, and doubts most things, nay, half disbelieves even his own existence.
Good-breeding differs, if at all, from high-breeding, only as it gracefully remembers the rights of others, rather than gracefully insists on its own.
Granted the ship comes into harbour with shrouds and tackle damaged; the pilot is blameworthy; he has not been all-wise and all-powerful; but to know how blameworthy, tell us first whether his voyage has been round the globe or only to Ramsgate and the Isle of Dogs.
Great is self-denial! Life goes all to ravels and tatters where that enters not.
Great is wisdom; infinite is the value of wisdom. It cannot be exaggerated; it is the highest achievement of man.
Great men are the fire-pillars in this dark pilgrimage of mankind; they stand as heavenly signs, ever-living witnesses of what has been, prophetic tokens of what may still be, the revealed, embodied possibilities of human nature.
Great Men are the inspired (speaking and acting) Texts of that Divine Book of Revelations, whereof a Chapter is completed from epoch to epoch, and by some named History.
Great men are the modellers, patterns, and in a wide sense creators, of whatsoever the general mass of men contrived to do and attain.
Great souls are always royally submissive, reverent to what is over them; only small, mean souls are otherwise.
Great, ever fruitful; profitable for reproof, for encouragement, for building up in manful purposes and works, are the words of those that in their day were men.
Gunpowder makes all men alike tall…. Hereby at last is the Goliath powerless and the David resistless; savage animalism is nothing, inventive spiritualism is all.
Habit and imitation are the source of all working and all apprenticeship, of all practice and all learning, in this world.
Habit is the deepest law of human nature.
Had not God made this world, and death too, it were an insupportable place.
Happy he for whom a kind heavenly sun brightens the ring of necessity into a ring of duty.
Happy men are full of the present, for its bounty suffices them; and wise men also, for its duties engage them. Our grand business undoubtedly is not to see what lies dimly at a distance, but to do what lies clearly at hand.
Happy season of virtuous youth, when shame is still an impassable celestial barrier, and the sacred air-castles of hope have not shrunk into the mean clay hamlets of reality, and man by his nature is yet infinite and free.
Has any man, or any society of men, a truth to speak, a piece of spiritual work to do; they can nowise proceed at once and with the mere natural organs, but must first call a public meeting, appoint committees, issue prospectuses, eat a public dinner; in a word, construct or borrow machinery, wherewith to speak it and do it. Without machinery they were hopeless, helpless; a colony of Hindoo weavers squatting in the heart of Lancashire.
Hatred is but an inverse love.
Have any deepest scientific individuals yet dived down to the foundations of the universe and gauged everything there? Did the Maker take them into His counsel, that they read His ground-plan of the incomprehensible All, and can say, This stands marked therein, and no more than this? Alas! not in any wise.
Have not all nations conceived their God as omnipresent and eternal, as existing in a universal Here, an everlasting Now?
He has verily touched our hearts as with a live coal from the altar who in any way brings home to our heart the noble doings, feelings, darings, and endurances of a brother man.
He is wise who can instruct us and assist us in the business of daily virtuous living; he who trains us to see old truth under academic formularies may be wise or not, as it chances, but we love to see wisdom in unpretending forms, to recognise her royal features under a week-day vesture.
He that can write a true book to persuade England, is not he the bishop and archbishop, the primate of England and of all England?
He that cannot be the servant of many will never be master, true guide, and deliverer of many.
He that cannot keep his mind to himself cannot practise any considerable thing whatever.
He that is the inferior of nothing can be the superior of nothing, the equal of nothing.
He who dwells in temporary semblances and does not penetrate into the eternal substance, will not answer the sphinx-riddle of to-day or of any day.
He who feels he is right is stronger than king’s hosts; he who doubts he is not right has no strength whatever.
“He who has been born has been a first man,” has had lying before his young eyes, and as yet unhardened into scientific shapes, a world as plastic, infinite, divine, as lay before the eyes of Adam himself.
He who has no vision of Eternity will never get a true hold of Time.
He who has not known poverty, sorrow, contradiction, and the rest, and learned from them the priceless lessons they have to teach, has missed a good opportunity of schooling.
He who in any way shows us better than we knew before that a lily of the fields is beautiful, does he not show it us as an effluence of the fountain of all beauty—as the handwriting, made visible there, of the great Maker of the universe?
He who traces nothing of God in his own soul will never find God in the world of matter—mere circlings of force there of iron regulation, of universal death and merciless indifferency.
He who wants everything must know many things, do many things to procure even a few; different from him whose indispensable knowledge is this only, that a finger will pull the bell!
He who will do faithfully needs to believe firmly.
Heat and darkness, and what these two may breed.
Here, on earth we are as soldiers fighting in a foreign land, that understand not the plan of the campaign, and have no need to understand it, seeing well what is at our hand to be done.
Hero-worship exists, has existed, and will for ever exist, universally among mankind.
Heroism, the Divine relation which, in all times, unites a great man to other men.
High air-castles are cunningly built of words, the words well-bedded in good logic mortar; wherein, however, no knowledge will come to lodge.
Histories are as perfect as the historian is wise, and is gifted with an eye and a soul.
History is an imprisoned epic, nay, an imprisoned psalm and prophecy.
History is the true poetry.
History, as it lies at the root of all science, is also the first distinct product of man’s spiritual nature, his earliest expression of what may be called thought.
Hitherto all miracles have been wrought by thought, and henceforth innumerable will be wrought; whereof we, even in these days, witness some.
Homer’s Epos has not ceased to be true; yet is no longer our Epos, but shines in the distance, if clearer and clearer, yet also smaller and smaller, like a receding star. It needs a scientific telescope, it needs to be reinterpreted and artificially brought near us, before we can so much as know that ’twas a sun…. For all things, even celestial luminaries, much more atmospheric meteors, have their rise, their culmination, their decline.
How beautiful to die of a broken heart on paper! Quite another thing in practice! Every window of your feeling, even of your intellect, as it were begrimmed and mud-bespattered, so that no pure ray can enter; a whole drug-shop in your inwards; the fore-done soul drowning slowly in a quagmire of disgust.
How blessed might poor mortals be in the straitest circumstances, if only their wisdom and fidelity to Heaven and one another were adequately great.
Apropos to his life at Craigenputtock.
How creatures of the human kind shut their eyes to the plainest facts, and by the mere inertia of oblivion and stupidity live at ease in the midst of wonders and terrors.
How hard it is (for the Byron, for the Burns), whose ear is quick for celestial messages, to “take no counsel with flesh and blood,” and instead of living and writing for the day that passes over them, live and write for the eternity that rests and abides over them!
How indestructibly the good grows, and propagates itself, even among the weedy entanglements of evil!
How many causes that can plead for themselves in the courts of Westminster, and yet in the general court of the universe and free soul of man, have no word to utter!
How much lies in laughter, the cipher-key wherewith we decipher the whole man.
How noble is heroic insight without words in comparison to the adroitest flow of words without heroic insight!
How noiseless is thought! No rolling of drums, no tramp of squadrons, or immeasurable tumult of baggage-waggons, attends its movements; in what obscure and sequestered places may the head be meditating which is one day to be crowned with more than imperial authority; for kings and emperors will be among its ministering servants; it will rule not over, but in all heads, and bend the world to its will.
How paint to the sensual eye what passes in the holy-of-holies of man’s soul; in what words, known to these profane times, speak even afar-off of the unspeakable?
How shall he give kindling in whose inward man there is no live coal, but all is burnt out to a dead grammatical cinder?
How they gleam like spirits through the shadows of innumerable eyes from their thrones in the boundless depths of heaven!
On the stars.
How we clutch at shadows (in this dream-world) as if they were substances, and sleep deepest while fancying ourselves most awake!
How were friendship possible? In mutual devotedness to the good and true, otherwise impossible; except as armed neutrality or hollow commercial league.
Human creatures will not go quite accurately together, any more than clocks will.
Human intellect, if you consider it well, is the exact summary of human worth.
Humour has justly been regarded as the finest perfection of poetic genius. He who wants it, be his other gifts what they may, has only half a mind; an eye for what is above him, not for what is about him or below him.
Humour is a sort of inverse sublimity, exalting, as it were, into our affections what is below us, while sublimity draws down into our affections what is above us.
Humour is properly the exponent of low things; that which first renders them poetical to the mind.
I have no notion of a truly great man that could not be all sorts of men.
I never heard tell of any clever man that came of entirely stupid people.
Ideals can never be completely embodied in practice; and yet ideals exist, and if they be not approximated to at all, the whole matter goes to wreck.
If “wise memory” is ever to prevail, there is need of much “wise oblivion” first.
If a book come from the heart, it will contrive to reach other hearts.
If a noble soul is rendered tenfold beautifuller by victory and prosperity, an ignoble one is rendered tenfold and a hundredfold uglier, pitifuller.
If cut (in the costume) betoken intellect and talent, so does the colour betoken temper and heart.
If in youth the universe is majestically unveiling, and everywhere heaven revealing itself on earth, nowhere to the young man does this heaven on earth so immediately reveal itself as in the young maiden.
If it is disgraceful to be beaten, it is only a shade less disgraceful to have so much as fought.
If Nature is one and a living indivisible whole, much more is mankind, the image that reflects and creates Nature, without which Nature were not.
If new-got gold is said to burn the pockets till it be cast forth into circulation, much more may new truth.
If one sees one’s fellow-creature following damnable error, by continuing in which the devil is sure to get him at last, are you to let him go towards such consummation, or are you not rather to use all means to save him?
If our era is an era of unbelief, why murmur at it? Is there not a better coming—nay, come?(
See Matt.
 v. 4.)
If the hungry lion (invited to a feast of chickenweed) is to feast at all, it cannot be on the chickenweed, but only on the chickens.
If the paternal cottage still shuts us in, its roof still screens us; and with a father we have as yet a prophet, priest, and king, and an obedience that makes us free.
If there be not a religious element in the relations of men, such relations are miserable and doomed to ruin.
If we do not now reckon a great man literally divine, it is that our notions of the divine are ever rising higher; not altogether that our reverence for the divine, as manifested in our like, is getting lower.
If you do not wish a man to do a thing, you had better get him to talk about it; for the more men talk, the more likely they are to do nothing else.
Imagination is but a poor matter when it has to part company with understanding.
Imperfections cling to a man, which, if he wait till he have brushed off entirely, he will spin for ever on his axis, advancing nowhither.
Impossible is the precept “Know thyself,” till it be translated into this partially possible one, “Know what thou canst work at.”
“Impossible,” when Truth and Mercy and the everlasting voice of Nature order, has no place in the brave man’s dictionary.
In a symbol there is concealment and yet revelation, silence and speech acting together, some embodiment and revelation of the infinite, made to blend itself with the finite, to stand visible, and, as it were, attainable there.
In a valiant suffering for others, not in a slothful making others suffer for us, did nobleness ever lie.
In all battles, if you await the issue, each fighter has prospered according to his right. His right and his might, at the close of the account, were the same.

Work is the cure for all the maladies and miseries of man—honest work, which you intend getting done.
Work is the mission of man on this planet.
Work, properly so called, is an appeal from the Seen to the Unseen—a devout calling upon Higher Powers; and unless they stand by us, it will not be a work, but a quackery.
Worship is transcendent wonder; wonder for which there is no limit or measure.
Wouldst thou plant for eternity? then plant into the deep infinite faculties of man, his fantasy and heart. Wouldst thou plant for year and day? then plant into his shallow superficial faculties, his self-love and arithmetical understanding, what will grow there.
Wrong is not only different from right, but it is in strict scientific terms infinitely different.
Yet a little while, and we shall all meet there, and our Mother’s bosom will screen us all; and Oppression’s harness, and Sorrow’s fire-whip, and all the Gehenna bailiffs that patrol and inhabit ever-vexed Time, cannot harm us any more.
You cannot abolish slavery by Act of Parliament, but can only abolish the name of it, which is very little.
You cannot have your work well done if the work be not of a right kind.
You cannot lead a fighting world without having it regimented, chivalried; nor can you any more continue to lead a working world unregimented, anarchic.
You feel yourself an exile in the East; but in the West too it is exile; I know not where under the sun it is not exile.
To a young friend.
You may paint with a very big brush, and yet not be a great painter.
Your rusty kettle will continue to boil your water for you if you don’t try to mend it. Begin tinkering and there is an end of your kettle.
